claim: Circadian rhythms are endogenous cycles in physiological, hormonal, and behavioral processes largely synchronized to the external 24 hr light-dark cycle.
source: Circadian rhythms are endogenous cycles in physiological, hormonal, and behavioral processes largely synchronized to the external 24 hr light-dark cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about circadian rhythms.

claim: The sleep-wake cycle is the most notable biological process that follows the 24 hr circadian rhythm.
source: The sleep-wake cycle is perhaps the most notable biological process that follows the 24 hr circadian rhythm (Zee and Vitiello, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zee and Vitiello, 2009.

claim: The timing of light exposure is the primary external driver of circadian rhythms.
source: The timing of light exposure is the primary external driver of circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about circadian regulation.

claim: Rapid changes in sleep timing can cause circadian misalignment through fluctuating light-dark exposure.
source: Therefore, rapid changes in sleep timing can cause circadian misalignment through fluctuating light-dark exposure (Zeitzer et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeitzer et al., 2000.

claim: Circadian misalignment is associated with several age-related diseases, including cancer and cardiovascular disease.
source: Circadian misalignment is associated with several age-related diseases, including cancer and cardiovascular disease (CVD) (Torquati et al., 2018; International-Agency-for-Research-on-Cancer, 2010; Janszky and Ljung, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Modern societal and lifestyle trends have blurred the distinction between day and night, increasing the propensity for circadian disruption.
source: However, the health impacts of irregular sleep-wake timing are still emerging. This remains an important area of study since modern societal and lifestyle trends, including exposure to artificial and blue light at night, longer work hours, shift work, and the 24-7 lifestyle, have blurred the distinction between day and night, increasing the propensity for circadian disruption (Walker et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 2020.

claim: Over 500,000 adults aged 40–69 years were recruited to the UK Biobank cohort between 2006 and 2010 across 22 assessment centers.
source: Over 500,000 adults aged 40–69 years were recruited to the UKB cohort between 2006 and 2010 across 22 assessment centers.
evidence: This is a factual description of the study cohort.

claim: The UK Biobank had a 5.5% participation rate.
source: Participants were invited by the UK National Health Service patient registers, resulting in a 5.5% participation rate.
evidence: This is a factual description of the study participation.

claim: UK Biobank respondents were more likely to be older, female, and less likely to live in socioeconomically deprived areas than the general population.
source: Respondents were more likely to be older, female, and less likely to live in socioeconomically deprived areas than the general population (Fry et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fry et al., 2017.

claim: A total of 106,053 participants completed a 7-day wrist-worn accelerometer study through random selection between February 2013 and December 2015.
source: A total of 106,053 participants completed a 7-day wrist-worn accelerometer study through random selection between February 2013 and December 2015.
evidence: This is a factual description of the accelerometry substudy.

claim: The sleep regularity index captures the probability of a participant being in the same state (asleep or awake) at any two time points 24 hr apart.
source: The SRI captures the probability of a participant being in the same state (asleep or awake) at any two time points 24 hr apart (Phillips et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2017.

claim: An individual who sleeps and wakes at precisely the same time each day would have a sleep regularity index of 100.
source: An individual who sleeps and wakes at precisely the same time each day would have an index of 100, whereas an individual who sleeps and wakes at entirely random times would have an index of 0.
evidence: This is a description of how the SRI metric is defined.

claim: An individual who sleeps and wakes at entirely random times would have a sleep regularity index of 0.
source: An individual who sleeps and wakes at precisely the same time each day would have an index of 100, whereas an individual who sleeps and wakes at entirely random times would have an index of 0.
evidence: This is a description of how the SRI metric is defined.

claim: Most UK Biobank participants (88%) provided complete accelerometry data.
source: Most participants (88%) provided complete accelerometry data.
evidence: This is a factual description of data completeness in the study.

claim: 88,975 (84%) participants provided valid SRI data and were included in the study.
source: In total, 88,975 (84%) participants provided valid SRI data and were included in the study.
evidence: This is a factual description of the final study sample.

claim: The mean sample age was 62 years (standard deviation 8).
source: The mean sample age was 62 years (standard deviation [SD], 8), 56% were women, and the median SRI was 60 (SD, 10).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study sample.

claim: 56% of the study sample were women.
source: The mean sample age was 62 years (standard deviation [SD], 8), 56% were women, and the median SRI was 60 (SD, 10).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study sample.

claim: The median SRI was 60 (SD, 10).
source: The mean sample age was 62 years (standard deviation [SD], 8), 56% were women, and the median SRI was 60 (SD, 10).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study sample.

claim: There were 3010 deaths during a mean follow-up of 7.1 years.
source: There were 3010 deaths during a mean follow-up of 7.1 years.
evidence: This is a factual description of mortality outcomes in the study.

claim: There is a non-linear relationship between the SRI and all-cause mortality hazard (p [global test of spline term]<0.001).
source: Following adjustments for demographic and clinical variables, we identified a non-linear relationship between the SRI and all-cause mortality hazard (p [global test of spline term]<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The hazard ratio for all-cause mortality was 1.53 (95% CI: 1.41, 1.66) for participants with SRI at the 5th percentile (SRI = 41) relative to the median SRI.
source: Hazard ratios, relative to the median SRI, were 1.53 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.41, 1.66) for participants with SRI at the 5th percentile (SRI = 41) and 0.90 (95% CI: 0.81, 1.00) for those with SRI at the 95th percentile (SRI = 75), respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The hazard ratio for all-cause mortality was 0.90 (95% CI: 0.81, 1.00) for participants with SRI at the 95th percentile (SRI = 75) relative to the median SRI.
source: Hazard ratios, relative to the median SRI, were 1.53 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.41, 1.66) for participants with SRI at the 5th percentile (SRI = 41) and 0.90 (95% CI: 0.81, 1.00) for those with SRI at the 95th percentile (SRI = 75), respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Findings for CVD mortality and cancer mortality followed a similar pattern to all-cause mortality.
source: Findings for CVD mortality and cancer mortality followed a similar pattern.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Irregular sleep-wake patterns are associated with higher mortality risk.
source: Conclusions:Irregular sleep-wake patterns are associated with higher mortality risk.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's data analysis.

claim: There were 3010 all-cause deaths during a median follow-up of 7.1 years (Q1, Q3: 6.6, 7.6).
source: There were 3010 all-cause deaths during a median follow-up of 7.1 years (Q1, Q3: 6.6, 7.6).
evidence: This is a factual description of mortality outcomes in the study.

claim: The most common primary cause of death was cancer (n=1701, 57%).
source: The most common primary cause of death was cancer (n=1701, 57%) followed by CVD (n=616, 20%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's mortality data.

claim: CVD was the second most common primary cause of death (n=616, 20%).
source: The most common primary cause of death was cancer (n=1701, 57%) followed by CVD (n=616, 20%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's mortality data.

claim: Mortality rates were highest among those with the most irregular sleep and decreased almost linearly as SRI approached its median, after which the decrease began to plateau.
source: Compared to the sample median (SRI = 61), mortality rates were highest among those with the most irregular sleep and decreased almost linearly as SRI approached its median, after which the decrease began to plateau (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis, supported by Figure 1.

claim: There was strong evidence against the proportionality assumption for all-cause mortality (p [time × SRI interaction]<0.001).
source: There was strong evidence against the proportionality assumption in the discrete-time hazards model (p [time × SRI interaction]<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: For the 5th percentile relative to the median SRI, hazard ratios for all-cause mortality were greatest in the earliest period of follow-up (HRs >2), declining until approximately 2.5 years, after which they remained approximately stable with an HR of around 1.5.
source: For the 5th percentile relative to the median, HRs were greatest in the earliest period of follow-up (HRs >2), declining until approximately 2.5 years, after which they remained approximately stable with an HR of around 1.5.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-varying hazards analysis.

claim: The SRI was associated with CVD-specific mortality in the primary model (p [global]<0.001).
source: The SRI was associated with CVD-specific mortality in the primary model (p [global]<0.001; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The hazard ratio for CVD mortality was 1.88 (95% CI: 1.61, 2.21) for the 5th percentile relative to the median SRI.
source: HRs, relative to the median SRI, were 1.88 (95% CI: 1.61, 2.21) and 0.93 (95% CI: 0.73, 1.20) for the 5th and 95th percentiles, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The hazard ratio for CVD mortality was 0.93 (95% CI: 0.73, 1.20) for the 95th percentile relative to the median SRI.
source: HRs, relative to the median SRI, were 1.88 (95% CI: 1.61, 2.21) and 0.93 (95% CI: 0.73, 1.20) for the 5th and 95th percentiles, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of non-proportional hazards for CVD mortality in the discrete-time hazards model (p [time × SRI interaction]=0.57).
source: There was no evidence of non-proportional hazards in the discrete-time hazards model (p [time × SRI interaction]=0.57).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Hazard ratios for low SRI were larger for females than males for CVD mortality (p interaction = 0.006).
source: HRs for low SRI were larger for females than males (p interaction = 0.006; Appendix 3—figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's interaction analysis.

claim: The SRI was associated with cancer mortality in the primary model (p [global]<0.001).
source: The SRI was associated with cancer mortality in the primary model (p [global]<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The hazard ratio for cancer mortality was 1.36 (95% CI: 1.22, 1.53) for the 5th percentile relative to the median SRI.
source: HRs, relative to the median SRI, were 1.36 (95% CI: 1.22, 1.53) and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.77, 1.02) for the 5th and 95th percentiles, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The hazard ratio for cancer mortality was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.77, 1.02) for the 95th percentile relative to the median SRI.
source: HRs, relative to the median SRI, were 1.36 (95% CI: 1.22, 1.53) and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.77, 1.02) for the 5th and 95th percentiles, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: There was strong evidence of non-proportional hazards for cancer mortality in the discrete-time hazards model (p [time × SRI interaction]<0.001).
source: There was strong evidence of non-proportional hazards in the cancer mortality discrete-time hazards model (p [time × SRI interaction]<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: For cancer mortality, hazard ratios for the 5th percentile vs. the median were large at the beginning of follow-up (HRs >2) and declined until approximately 4 years, after which they were small (~1.05) and compatible with the null.
source: HRs, for the 5th percentile vs. the median, were large at the beginning of follow-up (HRs >2) and declined until approximately 4 years, after which they were small (~1.05) and compatible with the null (Appendix 3—figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-varying hazards analysis.

claim: Results were similar and not meaningfully altered following adjustments for sleep time and WASO (Model 2).
source: Overall, results were similar and not meaningfully altered following adjustments for sleep time and WASO (Model 2) or history of disease at baseline, including cancer and CVD (Model 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: Results were similar and not meaningfully altered following adjustments for history of disease at baseline, including cancer and CVD (Model 3).
source: Overall, results were similar and not meaningfully altered following adjustments for sleep time and WASO (Model 2) or history of disease at baseline, including cancer and CVD (Model 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The SRI remained associated with mortality after further adjustments for disease history, BMI, systolic BP, BP treatment, and physical activity (Model 4), though effect sizes were attenuated.
source: The SRI remained associated with mortality after further adjustments for disease history, BMI, systolic BP, BP treatment, and physical activity (Model 4), though effect sizes were attenuated.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: When comparing the 5th percentile to the median in Model 4, the hazard ratio was 1.22 (95% CI: 1.07, 1.39) for all-cause mortality.
source: For example, when comparing the 5th percentile to the median, HRs were 1.22 (95% CI: 1.07, 1.39) for all-cause, 1.43 (95% CI: 1.21, 1.69) for CVD, and 1.15 (95% CI: 1.01, 1.29) for cancer mortality.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: When comparing the 5th percentile to the median in Model 4, the hazard ratio was 1.43 (95% CI: 1.21, 1.69) for CVD mortality.
source: For example, when comparing the 5th percentile to the median, HRs were 1.22 (95% CI: 1.07, 1.39) for all-cause, 1.43 (95% CI: 1.21, 1.69) for CVD, and 1.15 (95% CI: 1.01, 1.29) for cancer mortality.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: When comparing the 5th percentile to the median in Model 4, the hazard ratio was 1.15 (95% CI: 1.01, 1.29) for cancer mortality.
source: For example, when comparing the 5th percentile to the median, HRs were 1.22 (95% CI: 1.07, 1.39) for all-cause, 1.43 (95% CI: 1.21, 1.69) for CVD, and 1.15 (95% CI: 1.01, 1.29) for cancer mortality.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The SRI was modestly negatively correlated with the sleep duration SD (–0.32).
source: The SRI was modestly negatively correlated with the sleep duration SD (–0.32) and sleep onset time SD (–0.42; see correlation matrix in Appendix 3—table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The SRI was modestly negatively correlated with the sleep onset time SD (–0.42).
source: The SRI was modestly negatively correlated with the sleep duration SD (–0.32) and sleep onset time SD (–0.42; see correlation matrix in Appendix 3—table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: For each measure (SRI, sleep duration SD, sleep onset time SD), greater sleep irregularity was associated with an increased all-cause mortality rate in independent models (all p [global]<0.001).
source: For each measure, greater sleep irregularity (i.e., lower SRI or higher SD representing more day-to-day variability) was associated with an increased all-cause mortality rate in independent models (all p [global]<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: Hazard ratios for low regularity compared to the median were largest for the SRI compared to SD-based metrics.
source: HRs, for low regularity compared to the median, were largest for the SRI (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis, supported by Figure 3.

claim: The addition of the SRI to a model containing both SD metrics improved model fit (p [likelihood ratio test]<0.001).
source: The addition of the SRI to a model containing both SD metrics (alongside primary model covariates) improved model fit (p [likelihood ratio test]<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The addition of sleep duration SD and sleep onset time SD to a model containing the SRI did not meaningfully improve model fit (p [likelihood ratio test]=0.10).
source: Conversely, the addition of sleep duration SD and sleep onset time SD to a model containing the SRI (and primary model covariates) did not meaningfully improve model fit (p [likelihood ratio test]=0.10).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: Mutations or deletions to circadian clock genes such as CLOCK, PER, and BMAL1 influence BP, endothelial function, and glucose homeostasis.
source: Mutations or deletions to circadian clock genes such as CLOCK, PER, and BMAL1 influence BP, endothelial function, and glucose homeostasis (Viswambharan et al., 2007; Curtis et al., 2007; Anea et al., 2009; Rudic et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Both major (e.g., chronic shift work) and minor (e.g., daylight savings transitions) stressors to the circadian system have been associated with a higher risk of CVD.
source: Both major (e.g., chronic shift work) and minor (e.g., daylight savings transitions) stressors to the circadian system have been associated with a higher risk of CVD (Torquati et al., 2018; Janszky and Ljung, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Circadian clocks are critical to the orchestration of cell division.
source: For example, circadian clocks are critical to the orchestration of cell division (Reddy et al., 2005), and altered clock function can precipitate aberrant cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2016) as well as growth and DNA damage in cancer cells (Gery et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reddy et al., 2005.

claim: Altered clock function can precipitate aberrant cell proliferation.
source: For example, circadian clocks are critical to the orchestration of cell division (Reddy et al., 2005), and altered clock function can precipitate aberrant cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2016) as well as growth and DNA damage in cancer cells (Gery et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Altered clock function can precipitate growth and DNA damage in cancer cells.
source: For example, circadian clocks are critical to the orchestration of cell division (Reddy et al., 2005), and altered clock function can precipitate aberrant cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2016) as well as growth and DNA damage in cancer cells (Gery et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gery et al., 2006.

claim: Greater sleep-wake variability, as measured by the SD of sleep onset or duration, was independently associated with a higher risk of incident CVD in the multi-ethnic study of atherosclerosis but not the UK Biobank.
source: Whereas sleep regularity has not been examined with respect to incident cancer or mortality, the current findings extend research showing that greater sleep-wake variability, as measured by the SD of sleep onset or duration, was independently associated with a higher risk of incident CVD in the multi-ethnic study of atherosclerosis but not the UKB (Nikbakhtian et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Nikbakhtian et al., 2021 and Huang et al., 2020.

claim: The SRI may be superior to SD-based metrics because the SRI captures rapid changes in sleep patterns across consecutive days, as compared to the SD-based metrics which only calculate deviation from an individual's average.
source: The SRI may be superior to the SD-based metrics because the SRI captures rapid changes in sleep patterns across consecutive days, as compared to the SD-based metrics which only calculate deviation from an individual's average.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative analysis results.

claim: Rapid changes in sleep timing have been hypothesized as being principally challenging for the circadian system to accommodate.
source: Rapid changes in sleep timing have been hypothesized as being principally challenging for the circadian system to accommodate (Phillips et al., 2017) which may, in turn, produce negative health outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2017.

claim: Sleep of insufficient or excessive duration is associated with many adverse health outcomes, including increased mortality risk.
source: Sleep of insufficient or excessive duration is associated with many adverse health outcomes, including increased mortality risk (Cappuccio et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cappuccio et al., 2010.

claim: As of 2022, sleep duration was included by the American Heart Association in their Essential Eight guidelines for CVD prevention.
source: As of 2022, sleep duration was included by the American Heart Association in their Essential Eight guidelines for CVD prevention (Lloyd-Jones et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lloyd-Jones et al., 2022.

claim: The study was observational and therefore unable to establish cause and effect.
source: First, the study was observational. We are, therefore, unable to establish cause and effect.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the study design.

claim: Accelerometry is the recommended clinical tool for assessing circadian rhythms.
source: In addition, sleep diaries in the UKB were not available. Consequently, the algorithm we used to determine sleep and wake relied on the identification of a main 'sleep period time window' and did not identify napping.
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2018.

claim: The algorithm used to determine sleep and wake relied on the identification of a main 'sleep period time window' and did not identify napping.
source: Consequently, the algorithm we used to determine sleep and wake relied on the identification of a main 'sleep period time window' and did not identify napping.
evidence: This is a description of the study's methodology and its limitations.

claim: The findings were independent of several illness (including history of cancer and CVD at baseline), sleep duration, sleep fragmentation, and other confounding factors.
source: Our findings were independent of several illness (including history of cancer and CVD at baseline), sleep duration, sleep fragmentation, and other confounding factors.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings after adjustment for confounders.

claim: These data indicate a relationship between sleep regularity and longevity in a large community-based cohort.
source: Overall, these data indicate a relationship between sleep regularity and longevity in a large community-based cohort.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Irregular sleep may be a manifestation of the underlying physiological processes of cancer itself or of cancer treatment.
source: One plausible interpretation of this finding is that irregular sleep may be a manifestation of the underlying physiological processes of cancer itself or of cancer treatment (i.e., the SRI-cancer mortality association may be due to reverse causation).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the time-varying hazard ratios.

claim: A potential causal role of irregular sleep on CVD death cannot be easily ruled out.
source: In the case of CVD mortality, no such evidence of a decline in HRs over follow-up time was evident; a potential causal role of irregular sleep on CVD death cannot be easily ruled out.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of hazard ratios over time.

claim: Accelerometry data were collected using a wrist-worn device (Axivity AX3, United Kingdom) over a 7-day/night period.
source: Accelerometry data were collected using a wrist-worn device (Axivity AX3, United Kingdom) over a 7-day/night period.
evidence: This is a description of the study's data collection methodology.

claim: Estimated sleep status (awake or asleep) at a given time was calculated using the open-source R package GGIR version 2.7-1.
source: Estimated sleep status (awake or asleep) at a given time was calculated using the open-source R package GGIR version 2.7-1 (Migueles et al., 2019), using available algorithms (van Hees et al., 2015; van Hees et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the study's data processing methodology, supported by citations.

claim: GGIR uses an algorithm to determine a daily 'sleep period time window' for each participant.
source: To distinguish sleep from sustained periods of inactivity without reference to a sleep diary (not available in the UKB), GGIR uses an algorithm to determine a daily 'sleep period time window' for each participant (van Hees et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the GGIR algorithm, supported by citation.

claim: The algorithm does not, by default, detect bouts of sleep outside of the sleep period time window and hence is not able to identify naps.
source: The algorithm does not, by default, detect bouts of sleep outside of this window and hence is not able to identify naps.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the GGIR algorithm.

claim: Mortality occurrence was identified through linkage with NHS Digital for participants from England and Wales and the NHS Central Register for participants from Scotland, with complete records available until January 2022.
source: Mortality occurrence was identified through linkage with NHS Digital for participants from England and Wales and the NHS Central Register for participants from Scotland, with complete records available until January 2022.
evidence: This is a description of the study's mortality ascertainment methodology.

claim: ICD-10 codes I00-I99 and C00-C97 defined CVD and cancer mortality, respectively.
source: ICD-10 codes I00-I99 and C00-C97 defined CVD and cancer mortality, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the study's outcome definitions.

claim: Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine associations between the SRI and incident all-cause mortality, CVD mortality, and cancer mortality.
source: Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine associations between the SRI and incident all-cause mortality, CVD mortality, and cancer mortality.
evidence: This is a description of the study's statistical methodology.

claim: Surveillance for mortality commenced from the time of accelerometry (2013–2015) until the end of follow-up (January 2022), with a median follow-up time of 7.1 years (Q1, Q3: 6.6, 7.6).
source: Surveillance for mortality commenced from the time of accelerometry (2013–2015) until the end of follow-up (January 2022), with a median follow-up time of 7.1 years (Q1, Q3: 6.6, 7.6).
evidence: This is a description of the study's follow-up period.

claim: The SRI and all continuous confounders were modeled with restricted cubic splines with knots at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles to allow for departures from linearity.
source: The SRI and all continuous confounders were modeled with restricted cubic splines with knots at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles to allow for departures from linearity.
evidence: This is a description of the study's statistical methodology.

claim: Missing data were infrequent (<2%) for most confounder variables and were imputed (10 imputations) by predictive mean matching.
source: Missing data were infrequent (<2%) for most confounder variables and were imputed (10 imputations) by predictive mean matching using the aregImpute function of R package Hmisc (Harrell and Harrell, 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the study's handling of missing data.
